Post-translocation: Seed has not been located from other known sites in the region due to a range of environmental factors including prolonged torrential rain (flowers destroyed), flooding (loss of plants), drought since (no seed set). Given one plant only was translocated this loss will not have any impact on the over-all population of A. attenuata. column54: While Charlton East WR was also considered a fairly "safe" recipient site in terms of soil type and vegetation characteristics (as this reserve already supports a wild population of AJvS) there was some risk associated with heavy biomass cover and a higher position in the landscape than the wild population.  I did engage with the CFA Vegetation Management Officer to organise a pre-planting biomass reduction burn but unfortunately the officer was not able to make this happen in time.  This already heavy biomass cover was made worse by abundant spring rainfall in  2016. Seedlings from Nursery #1 were much larger and more robust at the time of planting than those from Nursery #2.  Given the biomass issues at this site I'm quite pleased with the moderate survivourship for this planting.

column54: Selection of Mt Doboobetic BR as a recipient site was a trade off between less-than-ideal soil type (i.e. cracking clay) vs. large remnant with relatively easily managed threats (biomass notwithstanding).  Mt Doboobetic was a bit of an experiment - while AJVS grows on sand dunes around Charlton, the southern populations around Bendigo grow on heavier soils.  Will be interesting to see whether any plants can persist here.  Seedlings from Nursery #1 were much larger and more robust at the time of planting than those from Nursery #2.  The low survivourship for this planting is disappointing but not wholly unexpected although it is good to see some seed production in the first summer post-planting.

column54: A significant challenge in Ballantinia reintroductions is that it is a tiny annual plant which lives in specialist habitat; establishment of a self-sustaining population is wholly dependent on annual germination and seed set which in turn is heavily influenced by winter rainfall.  With only low numbers of germinants in seed sowing trials the likelihood of success is small.  Further reintroduction plantings at Mt Alexander aren't really warranted at this stage as Ballantinia is more or less occupying all available and suitable remaining specialist habitat.  Future reintroduction efforts need to focus on suitable habitat away from Mt Alexander as a buffer against environmental catastrophe.

They looked reasonably good for the first months then started to fade and are now gone.
Competition was not an issue as most did not have new plants in the cleared area surrounding them.
Soil structure (previously deep drilled versus a subsample with shallow, little disturbed holes) did not result in any clear response difference.
Water may have been an issue, but if so then this time it was not the lack of water but potentially water logging (although that never seemed to be a problem on my inspections over the past months).
column54:
Many but not all of the native population are putting on new growth, in some instance luxuriantly so. One of the more interesting observations is that a medium-sized old plant growing practically at the base of a very large cypress pine is showing by far the mostly extensive new growth I have ever seen. Nearly a third of the otherwise healthy plant is soft.  
For the next attempt I would propose translocation near the native plants, with consistent small amounts of watering and weed control. The natives have thinned out enough that there are spaces where plants used to occupy. Although this would not give us the second site that we want for security, it would potentially inform us on future attempts elsewhere.

column54:
Following execllent success in seed orcharding (Ex CFC project at ANBG).
In partnership with Greening Australia and ANBG two translocations were conducted in winter 2013 into Reserves just outside the known distribution of the two extant populations. Site selection was based on spatial data. The 1589 plants were divided evenly between the two locations, were watered in at planting and on two following occasions. The plants were well established in large pots and had only been hardened off for a short period in the ANBG nursery. The project was an opportunistic one as a result of previous work that had been conducted by ANBG with the seed orchard and funding availability. The plants were potentially too large and not hardened off for long enough to increase the chance of survival. A very hot and dry summer followed, and no plants were observed as surviving by late summer 2014.

column54: 2015 was a supplementation project, so immediate proximity to the wild subpopulations was the key driver in site selection. column54: Can be established at new sites by either direct seeding or planting tube stock. However, tube stock provides a much more rapid means of establishing a new population. Tube stock allows a colony to be established more quickly through higher survivorship; that colony also produces more flowering plants and a higher number of flowers per plant than direct seeding in the first two years. Tube stock also reduces the impact of seed collection on in-situ populations because for each seed collected from the wild, more plants are established in the new populations using tube stock than are established using direct seeding. The planting of tube stock is the recommended method for future translocation projects involving R. leptorrhynchoides in the ACT.
